opening.headline: Although it is difficult to write examples of correct answers, we will learn how to improve the model when we can automatically determine whether the results are good or bad.
body: Whether the answer provided by the model satisfies the conditions can be determined using rules, code, or a separate review model, but it is difficult for a person to write down an ideal answer for each input in advance. Supervised fine-tuning is not well-suited to this task, as it requires a pair of inputs and ideal outputs to begin with.

Reinforced Fine Tuning (RFT) uses the value assigned to the model's answer by a scorer as a learning signal, rather than having the model follow examples of correct answers. In this class, we sequentially look at the learning flow leading to sampling, scoring, and updating, types of graders, reward design, and reward hacking that occurs when the grader is poor.

visual.alt: A picture showing two boxes side by side, showing that it is difficult to write a standard answer and that judging the result is possible.
labels: The two are not of the same level of difficulty.

paragraphs: A team is trying to create a model that automatically answers security questions from its customers. The question is, “Do you have a dedicated security team?” It is the same, and the model must return JSON containing `compliant` (yes, no, needs review) and `explanation` (reason explanation) based on the company policy document.

It is easy to determine whether the answer provided by the model satisfies the conditions. A string comparison is used to check whether the `compliant` value is as expected, and a separate screening model can read whether the description matches the policy and give a value between 0 and 1. On the other hand, for a person to write down an ideal answer to every question, expert consensus is needed, and there may be multiple appropriate expressions for the same question.

Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT) is a method that mimics pairs of inputs and ideal outputs, making it difficult to get started if such pairs are difficult to create in large quantities. So, is it possible to improve the model only with judgment criteria without examples of correct answers? This is the question this class addresses.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Writing the correct answer and determining whether it is correct have different levels of difficulty. This difference is the starting point of reinforced fine tuning.

screens.outro: First, let's think about whether there are jobs like this around you.

screens.title: Think about it: You can automate grading, but you can't write answers.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are there questions for which grading can be automated even if the correct answer cannot be written? Think about checking the output format.
items.answer: You can directly check with code whether the output complies with the JSON schema and whether field values are within the acceptable range. Even if you don't write down ideal sentences, rule violations are automatically identified.

items.prompt: How can I grade the results of tool calls?
items.answer: Simply compare the name and arguments of the called function to see if they are as expected. It is common to score the function name and arguments separately and combine them, and scoring is achieved even if there is no ideal answer sentence.

items.prompt: How do we grade work that does not have one correct answer, such as a summary?
items.answer: You can have the screening model evaluate with a value between 0 and 1 whether the summary contains all the items requested. Even if you don’t have to set up a standard summary, you can grade with just an evaluation rubric.

screens.outro: The method of using these automatic judgments as learning signals is enhanced fine tuning.

screens.title: Sampling, scoring, updating loop
screens.lead: Click the next button to follow the enhanced fine tuning process step by step. You can go back to the previous step with the previous button.

visual.alt: A circular diagram that goes from a prompt to a candidate answer, to a scorer, to a weight update, and back to the prompt.

steps.title: 1 Bring up the prompt
steps.body: Learning begins by pulling out one prompt from the prepared prompt dataset. All you need is a prompt and a reference value for the grader to use, not a single ideal answer. For the security question example, the question sentence and the expected value `compliant` would be one line of data.

steps.title: 2 Create multiple candidate answers
steps.body: The model generates multiple candidate answers for the same prompt. Even when asked the same question, some candidates have good reasoning and others have poor reasoning. This difference is needed to compare what is better, so if your evaluation results are always tied to the lowest or highest value, there is nothing to learn.

steps.title: 3 Grader gives rewards
steps.body: Each candidate answer is read by a user-defined scorer and assigned a numeric reward between 0 and 1. Some methods give only 1 for a correct answer, 0 for an incorrect answer, and others give an intermediate value for a partially correct answer. This number is the only learning signal that the model follows.

steps.title: 4 Update the weights
steps.body: With the policy gradient method, the model weights are slightly shifted so that outputs with high rewards are more likely to be produced and outputs with low rewards are less likely to be produced. It is important to make small changes several times rather than making big changes all at once.

steps.title: 5 Repeat until the end of data
steps.body: This cycle continues until the end of the training data and for the number of epochs you set. You can also evaluate intermediate checkpoints and stop when you are satisfied. Unlike SFT, which imitates a fixed standard answer, RFT learns by trying on its own through feedback called a scoring value.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at the different types of scorers that create training signals.

screens.title: Types and combinations of graders
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the composition and usage of each type of grader. Grader settings are written in JSON.

tabs.label: string_check
tabs.body:
It is the simplest scorer that returns 0 or 1 with a string comparison. `operation` uses `eq`, `ne`, `like`, and `ilike`. `like` and `ilike` check whether the input contains a reference, and `ilike` uses It is case insensitive. It's suitable for answers that are clear to pass or fail, such as city names, yes/no answers, or if they start with specific information.

```
{"type": "string_check", "name": "compliant",
 "operation": "eq",
 "input": "{{sample.output_json.compliant}}",
 "reference": "{{item.compliant}}"}
```

tabs.label: text_similarity
tabs.body: This is a scorer that quantifies how close the model output is to the reference sentence. Assign indicators like `evaluation_metric` to `fuzzy_match`, `bleu`, `gleu`, `meteor`, and `rouge_l`. It is good for open-ended answers where there is a paragraph-type reference answer written by an expert and you want to see how close it is to it. Remember that answers using different expressions for the same meaning may result in lower scores.

tabs.label: score_model
tabs.body: A separate screening model is a scoring machine that gives values within `range` determined according to the standards of the prompt. The input is a list of messages with `role` and `content`, within which you can use templates like `{{ item.reference_answer }}` or `{{ sample.output_text }}`. Non-numeric output is treated as 0, so you must tell the judging model to answer with only one number.

tabs.label: Python code
tabs.body: This is a scorer that calculates values by executing Python code you wrote yourself. Select this when the rule is complex and difficult to express through string comparison, or when the calculation result needs to be verified. Code has the advantage of being able to precisely control the decision logic, but if there is a loophole in the code, that loophole becomes a learning target.

tabs.label: multi
tabs.body: The `multi` scorer combines multiple scorers into one value. Insert a grader with a name in `graders`, and add weighted sums like `0.5 * compliant + 0.5 * explanation` in the formula `calculate_output`. When scoring a tool call, we combine a scorer that looks at the function name and a scorer that looks at the arguments: In the template, `item` refers to the dataset row and `sample` refers to the output produced by the model.

screens.outro: Now that we can combine scorers, let's move on to reward design, which determines which value to give higher.

screens.title: Compensation design and RFT fit together
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the rewards change when applying binary and partial grading to the same four candidate responses.

states.label: Partial grading (0 to 1)
states.body:
As in the security check example, assume that the `compliant` field is scored as `string_check`, and `explanation` is scored as `score_model`, adding 0.5 each. If the four candidates receive different values, such as 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0, information about which is better is conveyed closely. Candidates with correct answer fields but poor explanations also receive intermediate values, allowing the model to move towards improving the quality of explanations.

So what are the conditions for a problem that RFT is well suited for? The task must be unambiguous enough for experts to independently arrive at the same answer. The evaluation results should fluctuate rather than being tied to lows and highs, and the model should already be successful to some degree. Lastly, it must be a difficult-to-guess structure that does not result in high rewards even if guessed by chance.

states.label: Two-person scoring (correct/incorrect)
states.body:
If you score the same four candidates as 1 for correct and 0 for incorrect, the reward is divided into two values: 0, 0, 1, 1. Although the training signal is simple and easy to interpret, answers that are almost right and answers that are completely wrong equally receive 0. If it's a difficult task that the model rarely succeeds in the first time, then there are rare candidates that get a 1, so there are not enough signals to learn from.

If your model has a 0% success rate on this task, it cannot be pulled up to RFT. RFT is a method of sampling multiple answers, selecting the best ones, and changing them little by little, so from a starting point that never succeeds, there is nothing to strengthen. So, before RFT, we run an evaluation to check the current state of the model.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at the principles and design, let's look at an example to see what happens when the grader is sloppy.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Sloppy Graders and Reward Hacks
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case step by step. Click the Next button to follow how loopholes distort learning.

steps.title: Grading machine with loopholes
steps.body: Let's say the security question asks you to choose between `yes`, `no`, and `needs review`, and you only score `string_check`. Although it appears to be a clear scoring machine, there are actually only three options, so even if you take a picture without any basis, you will receive a reward with a probability.

steps.title: model's reaction
steps.body: The model works based on the conditions under which the grader rewards you, not the intent of the task. Since it is more efficient to make frequent, rewarded single-word guesses than to make long inferences, the tendency to make shorter inferences and single-word guesses becomes stronger as learning progresses.

steps.title: Definition of Rewards Hacking
steps.body: This phenomenon in which the model optimizes for loopholes in the grader rather than the intent of the task is called reward hacking. The risk is that the reward value increases but the actual quality does not, making it seem like success just by looking at the learning curve.

steps.title: loophole in the opposite direction
steps.body: Conversely, there are cases where the grader is too strict and cuts off normal answers. If you compare function arguments only by string matching, you will receive virtually the same value, such as `1` and `1.0`, or 0 if the state name is abbreviated. In this case, the model will be punished even if it gives the correct answer.

steps.title: How to Complement
steps.body: Change it to a structure that is difficult to guess. Break down classes into subclasses or require open-ended answers instead of multiple-choice answers. The parts missed by strict comparison are complemented by the `text_similarity` or `score_model` scorer, and combined with the `multi` scorer, they cover each other's loopholes. After supplementing, before starting training, check with a few inputs that the grader gives the values ​​as intended.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the types of loopholes, let's summarize the criteria for determining which questions can be graded.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Differentiating gradable and non-gradable problems
screens.lead: The instructor applies the same judgment questions to three tasks. Click the Next button to see how the judgments are divided for each task.

steps.title: Three Judgment Questions
steps.body: There are three questions: First, do experts independently converge on the same answer? Second, can it be expressed as a scoring option? Third, do the evaluation results fluctuate rather than being tied to the lowest or highest? Gemini's reward functions are also divided into function-based, LLM-based, and user-defined methods, and the same questions apply.

steps.title: Task A: Match fields in structured output
steps.body: The task of checking whether fields in the output JSON are equal to expected values is converged by an expert, expressed as `string_check` or a code scorer, and there is some variation as the model gets some things right and some things wrong. Judgment can be automated.

steps.title: Task B: Select relevant passages from legal precedents
steps.body: Scoring is possible if there is a consensus among experts to select the same passages. On the other hand, if the passages that each expert views as important are different, the task is ambiguous and the problem needs to be redefined. Judgment is conditional. We need to first check if there is an agreement.

steps.title: Task C: Assessing writing styles of varying tastes
steps.body: Different people have different standards for good writing style, so experts do not agree. Even if you score with a screening model, the standard is shaken, resulting in different values ​​for the same answer, and that shake becomes noise in the reward signal. The verdict is not suitable for RFT. Refine your rubric or consider another approach.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: Whether grading is possible is determined not by whether the correct answer can be written, but whether people agree on the criteria for judging. And only when the standards are accurately transferred to the grader can the quality of RFT be secured. This is why we say that the quality of an RFT is the quality of its grader.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's summarize the key points and apply them to our work.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We summarize what we have seen so far in one flow. Read slowly and check how each paragraph connects to the content on the previous screen.

paragraphs: Rather than imitating the correct answer, RFT allows the model to try multiple answers and reinforce the best ones with rewards given by a scorer. So what you need are prompts and grading criteria, not a single ideal answer.
The grader is the learning objective. A sloppy scorer invites reward hacking, while a too-strict scorer discounts good answers. So designing and checking the scorer takes up most of the RFT work.

Applicability falls into three categories: Check whether the task is converging on experts, whether it is expressed in scoring options, whether there is variation in the evaluation results, and whether the model already has some success.

Going back to the question in this class, even if you can't write down the correct answer, if people can agree on the criteria and transfer that criteria to the grader, there is a way to improve the model. Conversely, if the standard is unstable, no matter how sophisticated the scorer is, the learning signal becomes noise.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Remember that RFT targets an inference model and is a way for the inference process to be strengthened.

checks.intro: Check for yourself the learning principles you just learned. Grading values ​​are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the biggest difference between enhanced fine tuning (RFT) and supervised fine tuning (SFT)?
options: For each input, we set one ideal output as the correct answer and learn to imitate it.
Create multiple candidate answers and adjust the weights so that output with a higher reward value given by the grader is better.
Update the model only with pre-trained knowledge without training data
Learning can only proceed if a person directly ranks each candidate answer.
checks.explain: In RFT, a scorer gives reward values to the candidate answers produced by the model, and shifts the weight so that highly rewarded outputs appear more often. The source of the learning signal is different from SFT, which follows a fixed standard answer.

wrong.0: This is the SFT way. RFT is learned through graded feedback rather than imitation of standard answers.
wrong.2: It requires training input, such as prompts and grading criteria, and will not update without input.
wrong.3: Ranking is not done by humans, but a grader automatically gives reward values.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. We correctly pointed out that the learning signal comes from the grader's reward, not the standard answer.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's a pity. Recall where the learning signals for both methods come from.

checks.q: When asked to choose one of the yes/no/needs reviews and scored only with string_check, the model tended to select one word without inference. What explanation best fits this situation?
options: Since the reward value has increased, the intention of the task has been learned well.

It's a compensation hack where the model optimizes for loopholes in the scorer, not what it's intended to do.

wrong.0: If the grader is poor, the reward value will only increase and the task may not work out well.
wrong.1: It's not about learning speed, it's about reward structure.

glossary.def: This is a tuning method that updates the inference model little by little using the compensation signal provided by the scorer. Instead of imitating correct answer examples, it learns to produce better output with high rewards.
A rule, code, or triage model that evaluates the model output with a number such as 0 to 1. In RFT, this defines the learning objectives.
It is a matter of deciding what to give a high value to and how to assign partial grading and weighting.
This is a phenomenon that only increases the reward value by targeting loopholes in the grading machine instead of the intent of the work.
This is an update method that moves model weights so that output with high rewards is better.

misconceptions.myth: RFT also requires an ideal correct answer for each input.
misconceptions.fact: The key to RFT is the prompt and scoring criteria. Reference values ​​in the dataset are only needed for use by the grader, and there is no need to write down a single ideal answer.

misconceptions.myth: If the reward value increases, you have done a good job.
misconceptions.fact: If the grader is poor, it may be a reward hack that only increases the reward value. The increase in value and the actual improvement in quality must be checked separately.

misconceptions.myth: RFT can be applied to any model.
misconceptions.fact: RFT targets inference models, and if the model has a 0% success rate on the task, it has no starting point and is unlikely to be effective.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: RFT learns through a cycle of sampling, scoring, and updating.
The quality of your RFT depends on the quality of your scorer.
Scoring possibilities are determined by expert consensus, variation in evaluation results, and avoidance of guesswork.
Poor graders lead to reward hacking.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Can our questions be automatically graded? If possible, which combination of scorers best captures the intent?
